blocks.x: Jimmy Rowles (Sept. 27, 1984):
I was born in Spokane, Washington, 1918, August 19th. And the story goes from there. How does that sound?
Well, this is September 27, 1984, I'm Dan Morgenstern, and we are talking to Jimmy Rowles. [ETC.]
So we said the story goes from there. Spokane is where Bing Crosby was born, right?
Right.
Was your family musical?

My mother was. See, my father died when I was three months old. So I never had a father. I had a stepfather. And he was very un-musical. He wanted me to do all kinds of things that I didn't want to do, like caddie for him every Sunday, when I was a... I was a tennis player, and I don't mind saying I was a good one, and I won a few tournaments in my time up there. But on Sundays, when all the good players were playing, I was out on the golf course carrying his clubs. And he was a dubber. And we never really had anything tight together.

So when I finally got to be twenty-one years old, he was sending me to law school; he was going to make a lawyer out of me. And I had been practicing, trying to learn how to play like Teddy Wilson. And when I got to be twenty-one years old, I just said, with the help of my wife, who I was
Rowles - 2

going with... She said, "Just tell him what you want to do." So I stood just up at the dinner table and said, "I'm going to make an announcement..." I was scared to death of the guy. He never touched me. And I just said, "I am going to Los Angeles tomorrow morning. I've got twenty-five dollars; that's all I've got. But I have a ride. And I'll see you all later. And as far as being a lawyer is concerned, forget it. I'm going to Los Angeles and see if I can make it in the music business. I don't know what I'm want to do, but I'm going to play that piano -- that's what I'm gonna do."
And he said, "Don't expect anything from me." And I never corresponded with him, he never corresponded with me; and that was the end of that. I saw him a couple of times. That's it.

So I went to Los Angeles. I didn't know anybody there. I had to do an awful lot of walking. And I started going up to Harlem, up to Watts, every night late... First I'd make all the clubs in Hollywood, and there was one or two or three that would let me sit in. Then I'd catch the last train, streetcar, out to Watts down by City College, and I'd go out and stay there all night. And when it was all over, I'd take the streetcar, come all the way back home, and go to bed. I was living in a boarding house, eight dollars a
Rowles - 3

week, board and room.
And every night I did the same thing, until finally a piano player... At one of the places they used to let me sit in, the piano player, for some reason, got something else and he quit. And I still had two weeks to go on my six months; they had a thing there that ....(?).... six months before you had take a steady job. And I had two weeks to go, and he got permission, and they hired me. And that was my first job in Los Angeles, steady job, with a bass, tenor saxophone and piano.
Who were the guys?

The guys were King Guyon(?) and a bass player named Bob Straw. And I don't know what happened to either one of them. I really don't. I know that Bob Straw married the waitress, and King Guyon(?) is supposed to have married some wealthy woman and moved back east here somewhere. I don't know. And I have never seen either one of them since.
Then this drummer started coming in, and he got me with bands he was playing with. He was playing with Mugsy Marcellino and Garwood Vann, and he got me in there -- and I started to play with those two bands.
Then I met this one girl... It's funny, years and years later, she eventually ended up marrying Rex Stewart. Her name was Claire Fisher. And she had a car, evidently had
Rowles - 4

money -- I didn't have any money. I was working by then... The drummer had gotten himself a job, and he had a five-piece band, and I was in it. And Claire used to come over to where... I was staying at his house then; I'd moved in with him. And she used to come and take me, and she took me around to different places -- and she took me to hear Slim and Slam. And I sat in and played with them. Then they hired me, added me to their trio -- made a trio out of it. And I played for them quite a while.
Was that at Billy Berg's?

No. It was before Billy Berg's. It was a place down on Eighth Street. The guy's name was Herb Rose. He had a club there. He used to have Nat Cole and this and that. I think his mother was frightened by a cash register, because [LAUGHING] this one night, business was bad, and he used to... He was always on the waitresses, you know, like "That guy's drink is half-gone, go get him" -- all that junk. Because he was really hungry.

And this one night there wasn't anything going on. Nat Cole and his trio, his original trio were up there singing "Sweet Lorraine" and stuff. And who comes in and sits down at the bar but Carlos Castel, the Brain. And we got to talking with this guy, and first thing you know, the guy says, "I'd sell his contract for ten dollars." The guy said
Castel
Rowles - 5

"Oh yeah?" Carlos says, "Right now." So he whips out the ten dollars and says, "Give me the contract." And from that moment, Carlos Gastel owned Nat Cole. So the first thing he did was take him up to Capitol and have him make "Nature Boy," and that was the beginning of Nat Cole -- Carlos Gastel. Isn't that wild?
Yeah.

Oh, that guy used to scream about that, that Herb Rose. He had Tatum, everybody in there. I played intermission piano for Tatum in there! Do you believe that? I used to sit outside. I wouldn't go in. I would wait for the streetcar to take me home, and he'd drag me in there and make me play while Art was taking a vacation at intermission.

So then that one folded some way, and I went over to play up at some joint that Tatum used to play. That's where I met Art. And things progressed, and I'd take jobs and worked here and there, around town. And I was becoming pretty well-known, you know... "That new guy that's in town, that guy with the rosy cheeks, he plays pretty good." So this and that, and I was workin'...
And finally, I got a call from Billy Berg. He wanted me to join a band with a Slim and Slam, and Lee and Lester Young, Bumps Meyers, and Jake Porter and Eddie Beal, the
Rowles - 6

Spirits of Rhythm -- a great big conglomeration thing. And he was going to pay forty dollars a week or something like that. Which was great with me. I mean, I'd be having fun. So I took it. And I worked out there...

We worked in a place called the Capri. And we had Big Joe Turner singin' the Blues, and Ray Bryant was dancing, and we traded off sets, you know, with Lee and Lester Young and Slim and Sam's band, alternating with Spirits of Rhythm with Teddy Bunn and Leo Watson, and Big Joe Turner was singing with them... I got to know an awful lot of people. Ben Webster used to come in. I had met Ben previously in Seattle, and we became very close, and he used to come out there all the time and play with us. And he kept telling me, you know, he says, "I'm gonna get you with Benny Goodman if it's the last thing I do." And he did. He got his chance.

We switched clubs, and moved down to Fairfax and Beverly into a place called the Trouville, and they changed everything all around. It became Lee and Lester Young's band without Slim and Sam. That's where I met Red Callender and Louis Gonzales, a guitar player, and a trumpet player from St. Louis who used to be with Basie, Paul Campbell, and Lester and Bumps, Lee, and me -- we were the band. Slim and Slam played alone, and the Spirits of Rhythm played alone,
Rowles - 7

Ray Bryant and Big Joe Turner. Then later on, Barney Bigard left Duke Ellington for a while, and he came in with a group -- well, I think he played with the Spirits of Rhythm. That was about the time Jimmy Blanton died.

Anyway, from there... I was working there, and I had been working... And Billie Holiday came out and joined us; that's where I met her. That's where I started learning how to accompany, by listening to her and... I literally fell in love with her, not sexually, just brother-sister.

I thought that everybody expected a big sexual thing with she and Lester Young when she showed up. But it was not that way. It was brother and sister. Because he had a girl named Teddy, Teddy Bear, and she was there almost every night. I still talk to her out in Los Angeles. She's somebody you should talk to. She could tell you more about Lester Young than anybody. And I can give you her telephone number, Teddy Bear. She's usually stoned, but she makes a lot of sense. But she's a wonderful woman. So when you come out there in October, you call me and I'll give you her telephone number, and you can go out and visit with her a little bit. She'll tell you some things about Lester Young that nobody knows, nobody will ever know unless she says it, because she lived with him. She was his old lady.
All those tenor players used to come out there with
Rowles - 8

blood in their eye. Didn't make any difference. Every one of them, he blew 'em all out. Illinois Jacquet, Don Byas, Ben Webster, Willie Smith, Joe Thomas... Hawk never showed up. He never was in town. But everybody that showed up, he wound up blowin' 'em clear out of the place. And he was practically on his face before they even showed... He used to drink like crazy. He was already four feet off the ground when they showed up sober! Then he'd finish 'em off one by one. Never a bad word about 'em. They all put him down, but he never put them down. I never heard him put anybody down

So then I got my chance. One of the waitresses said that a guy wanted to talk me. And it was Benny's brother; and Benny wanted me. Then Jimmy Maxwell, the first trumpet player with Benny Goodman... Benny and Mel Powell had had a fight, and they were through. So Jimmy Maxwell was a good friend of Ben Webster's, and he talked to him about it, and he got me the job -- Ben told him to get me.

Because they were coming to California to make a picture anyway. So they sent ahead and they got me. And I stayed with him about...oh, four or five months. He was suffering from sciatica, which I knew nothing about. No wonder he was hard to get along with. And he was constantly using that ray, you know, and whenever he would find anybody
Rowles - 9

that he could get away with on it... And he used it on me, and I got mad. I didn't like it. And I didn't... I had gone on the wagon, because I wanted to play good for him. But I decided to go with the guys finally at intermission and started going across the street, and then I'd come back and then I'd put him on, play and all that... I almost had a fist-fight with him one night, begged him to fire me...

And then I finally got a chance to go with Woody Herman, so I quit. And it was just like goin'...jumpin' into Heaven to go with Woody Herman. That's why ....(?). ... became one of my best friends. And Hazel Scott was the final on the stage. She had Big Sid Catlett; I got to know him when I was over there playing.
And I stayed with Woody... That was a good band. He was changing the band, and buying the guys... It was a cooperative band, see, and he was buying the guys out one by one.
That was sort of the transition between the First and the Second Herd.

Right. Right. The band that played the Blues into more of an Ellington thing. And just as it was getting... He had the hottest band in the country at the time that they took me, then all of a sudden they snatched me and grabbed me and put me in the Army -- three years.
Rowles - 10

And the day I got out of the Army, the day I got my discharge, I got a call from Woody to come back. So I came back, and I stayed with Woody until he broke up his band because of financial problems. Then I went to Los Angeles and stayed. Then he re-formed.

In the meantime, I worked with Tommy Dorsey down at the Beach. I worked with Les Brown at the Palladium. Benny Goodman came out to do a radio show with Victor Borge, and he hired me. Heh, I couldn't believe it, but he did. And he didn't even remember...you know, he's a little bit foggy at times. But I didn't ...(?). . .(?). . .

Let's see, then what happened... Oh yeah, then we were doing this... Oh yeah, I got a call to go back with the Four Brothers Band for Woody, and I turned it down -- I didn't want any more of that road. No, no. And I'm glad I didn't go, because there were too many junkies there, and it might have turned me into a junkie. And I'm glad I didn't go. Herb Steward couldn't stand it, and he quit.
Yeah, that was a wild crew in that band.

Oh God! That was unbelievable, that band. Guys nodding out and all that. I wouldn't be in the band. No, I would have quit, like Herbie ...(?). . .(?). . . And Herbie hasn't done too much since that. He can still play, though. He lives around Frisco.
Rowles - 11
Yeah, once in a while he makes a record or something, and he still sings...

Yeah. I made a record with him where he played alto and flute, with Barney Kessel. Not too long ago, a couple of years ago... More than that. Five or six or seven years ago. He sounds beautiful. But he's around Frisco, and he's still playing very, very pretty. In fact, of all the solos on Four Brothers, I'll take his. It's the prettiest.

And so, I turned that job down. I'm stayin' in L.A. I'm not going anywhere. And I was existing, and I was happy; you know, I'd play with these different bands and stuff, you know. So all of a sudden, I get the call from Jerry Gray to play the Bob Crosby Radio Show, and that lasted for four years. And that's when I started recording, with the Modernaires, during the late Forties, about '47 or something like that. Then I started making recordings, and people started hiring me for recordings.

Then I went to Vegas with Peggy Lee on a vacation type thing, and she at the end of it took me out to Fox, and I met Alfred Newman -- and he heard me play. He said he liked the way I played. And the first thing you know, I was working at Fox and recording. And the next thing you know, I was doing different studios, and the first thing you know,
Rowles - 12
I was a studio man! I was just busy as a bee. I was what they called hot. I played all over. I played all the studios. They used to feature(?) me...

Then I went to work at Universal; I used to do an awful lot of work at Universal. That's where Hank Mancini heard me, and he hired me, and I worked for Hank, not on a... I was his pianist. I worked for him for seventeen years. But all we did was pictures and concerts. So it wasn't like a steady job, you know. Like, if you were to exist on the money you made with Hank Mancini, you'd starve. But whenever you did work with Mancini, you made money. You had a three-day picture, and then the next week you'd make an album of the picture, and then in the meantime he'd do the Hollywood Bowl or the Shrine Auditorium or something like that. And I was his pianist, and I made all his records. That went on for seventeen years.

And in the meantime, I was doing all the rest of this studio work -- jingles and record dates and Nelson Riddle and Billy May and you name it, with everybody...even Pete Rugolo. You name it. I was in there. I was hot. And it was driving me crazy. I finally took a staff job at NBC, and signed up for three years.
There was a club across the street where a guy let me form a Jazz trio, playing two nights a week, Sunday and
Rowles - 13

Monday. And I got these two guys. First I started with Red Mitchell and Nick Martinez; and then Red got a chance to do something else that was better, and I got Max Bennett -- so I had those two guys for a while. And the trio, we used to work around whenever we could.

Then I switched drummers, and I had a little set-to with Max Bennett, and all of a sudden I was without my trio. But this guy called me down at the Beach, so I got Andy Simpkins and Stix Hooper. And we worked up a tremendous trio. Andy... Well, you know who they are.
Sure.

So all of a sudden, somebody shows up and brings in George Shearing to listen to this trio, and it just so happened that he was looking for a drummer and a bass -- and there went my bass and drums. And then I'm dead again.

So now I go through about six bass players, and I finally got Monty Budwig. And we were having our problems with the drums. I couldn't depend on Frank Butler, because he'd sell his drums; he was sick, you know, with the needle.
A terrific drummer.
He was one of the best drummers around. It's just too bad. It's a tragedy. And he died... Yeah, he was one of my very, very good friends, and he was a tremendous
Rowles - 14

drummer.
Well, that job lasted quite a while. I kept switching drummers. I can't remember who I'd find... I finally got Donald Bailey. That was my favorite. He is my favorite drummer, Donald Bailey -- and I got him. And that was the beginning of my trio. Probably the best trio I ever had was Donald Bailey and Monty Budwig. And then I started writing out some real bass parts. I didn't write drum parts in those days. And no piano parts. So nobody could steal the library, because nobody knew what the heck the tunes were. I was writing out all the Wayne Shorter tunes, and all the Jazz tunes I'd hear on the records, you know, from Horace Silver and everybody, you know...
We had a helluva trio. And all the drummers would come around: "Where in the world did you get that drummer." I'd say, "Never mind. I got him. You keep your hands off him. He's my drummer."
Then I started working with singers more and more. I went to work with Peggy. I worked with Peggy, Peggy Lee for about five years...
Did you go on the road with her?
Mmm-hmm. I worked The Andy Williams Show. After they had cut the staff off, they kept an orchestra for Andy Williams, and I played for him for about five or six
Rowles - 15
years. Then I played for Vic Damone, and here and there, and different guys, different shows around town -- I played for all the major singers. I even played for Martha Raye one time. Enjoyed that.
She's a good singer.
You're darn right she's a good singer. Great lady, too.

Then I took this job at the beach, way down on Manhattan Beach with my trio. And about that time, Sarah Vaughan and Carmen McRae moved into town. They weren't doing too much, so they used to come on down all the time an sing with me. And I'd go home to either one of their houses and stay there after work, you know, and talk it up and everything, and raise a lot of heck -- and I wound up making some records with them. I made "The Great American Songbook" with Carmen, and I made a record with Sass, Sarah, "Sarah Vaughan with Jimmy Rowles' Rhythm Section." I don't think they made too many pressings on that one.

But the guy from Amsterdam, Root de Toot(?), or whatever his name is, Root de Voot(?)... I never did get to meet him. Because he wanted the whole group that made the record where she sang "Thelonious Monk," which was my song, and everybody chickened out but me. Because I wanted to see Ben Webster. I hadn't seen him. And he was in Copenhagen.
Rowles - 16

So when we finished playing the concert in Amsterdam, she gave me some time off, which was very extraordinary. I didn't have to be back until the day after my birthday. So I said, 'That's just great.' So I went to Copenhagen, surprised Ben, stayed with him for a little over a week. And, 'Ta-ta, I've got to go back.' I got back to Belgium, and there was no message, they hadn't taken care of my room, which they were supposed to do -- I had to pay for that. Then I got mad, so I just had my ticket changed. So I didn't go to Amsterdam and went right straight back to New York. Then I stayed here about two or three days, then I went right straight to Los Angeles.

Then I'm sitting in Los Angeles and I got a call from Root(?) in Copenhagen. Ben had had a stroke and died in Amsterdam. So at least I got to see Ben the last couple of weeks before he died. He was like my father.

So then I came back, and I went into the studios and back with ...(?)... and this and that -- and I was sick and tired of the studios. And I had an opportunity to play the Jazz Festival back here, the tribute to Art Tatum, so I took it. Then that gave me a week with a trio at...
The Cookery?
No, the other one. Uptown. [ETC.]
Anyway, I worked up there for a week. Then I went back
Rowles - 17

to Los Angeles. Then I got a call from the Cookery for seven weeks. So I went to the Cookery. I used to start hanging around at Bradley's. Then the first thing you know, I'm working at Bradley's... And the first thing you know, I'm working at Bradley's, and I stumbled around New York for about five-six-seven years, where I got to know people like you and... I didn't know anybody, you know. I was a lonesome polecat from L.A., buried in the studios.
You know most of what went on from there...
Right.

Finally, I stayed here... Then finally Norman Granz called me. And I didn't realize how I was getting. Then I took this job with Ella. I didn't know anything about what her schedule was. I didn't realize how much traveling she did and what it was like. I was with her for two years, and it almost killed me. I wound up with emphysema, and I had to quit. So I went to Los Angeles, and, I was old enough to qualify for unemployment...
You mean Social Security.
Yeah, Social Security. And I started getting that. I just didn't want to play, anyway.
Then I started listening to Stacy, my daughter. She gave me an incentive, and I started writing things for her to play -- and we started playing jobs around town a little
Rowles - 18

bit. And we're still doing it. We just played a very successful couple of weeks down here at Merkle's(?), and right now we're working at Hanratty's, just the two of us. Our plans are to... I would like to play... Instead of playing clubs, where... See, I'm sixty-six years old right now. And with this problem I have, I just can't work six nights a week, every night, and travel all over the place. I've got to work out some kind of thing where all I do is play concerts or go someplace for maybe one or two days, and then take off for a month and...take it easy, you know. Because I've got to hold on to whatever I've got left.
But she's... You know, you've heard her play. She's probably one of the most marvelous trumpeters, for a woman... You very, very seldom hear a girl who can play like that.
Did you have a lot to do with Stacy getting started in music?

Oh yeah. I was sitting on the davenport one afternoon. And there was a trumpet player out in Los Angeles who was an old friend of mine, and he'd given me a trumpet... Because I used to play trumpet in the Army, to keep from the gun. So he gave me this trumpet. So she brought it down... She went up to the attic and she found it, and she brought it down, and she said, "Can you play
Rowles - 19

this?' [LAUGHS] I said, 'Sure I can play it. Give it to me.' So I played it for her. She said, 'Show me how to play it.' So I showed her the embrochure, which Chuck Peterson had taught me in the Army, a good embrochure, the right kind, and I showed her the chromatic scale. And up she goes, back up to the attic, and she started. And every time I'd drive into the driveway, I'd hear this trumpet. And the first thing I know, she comes home, she's saying, 'Pop, I'm in the band' -- fifth trumpet or something like that.
How old was she then?

Oh, she was about fifteen. She was in junior high school. Then she just kept moving. They moved up to fourth trumpet, third trumpet, second... Then she got hot on the flugelhorn; she wanted a flugelhorn for her birthday. So I bought her a flugelhorn. And I'll be darned if she didn't go down to Costa Mesa, where they have a big conglomeration of bands and everything, and she won first place in the Soloists contest, and they gave her another flugelhorn -- the same kind, a Quinyan(?). Of course, the guy at the school that had the band was a real bad guy, and he wanted her to donate it to the school. And you know what I told him, or told her to tell him. And she did.
So she just kept getting better and better. Then she
Rowles - 20

met Clark Terry... She knows all of them...you know, Freddie Hubbard... I don't know if she knows Wynton Marsalis or not. She knows Dizzy very well, you know... And they all respect her very highly. And we just made this album called Tell It Like It Is, and everybody seems to like it.
Oh yes, a lovely album.
You don't happen to have it?
I do.
You do have it.
Yes.
Ah. Well, I was going to give you one.
No, I get...Carl Jefferson... They send me records. I was very pleased to get it. I got it about a week ago or so...
[PAUSE]

...but when I was a kid, though, you know, before I ever heard Teddy Wilson play the piano, I was a Lombardo freak. I loved him. And I loved Carmen Lombardo singing. I loved Liebert. I loved everybody. I knew everybody's name. I was their number-one fan!
Had you seen the band?
Yeah, I saw them once, when they came to my home town. And they didn't even... Not one of them got out one piece of music during the night. And they played more
Rowles - 21

tunes that night than any band I ever heard in my life, going from one to the next. I loved their piano player, Freddie Kreitzer. In fact, I even called him here. I got loaded one night here in New York, and called him in Florida. He didn't believe me at all! He says, "You mean, that Jazz piano player?" "Yup, that's me." He didn't think it was me.
What was it you liked about the band most?

I liked their sound, and I liked their... They were so crisp. That's what I liked about Hal Kemp. They were together. There was nothin' sloppy about it. And yet, when Count Basie's first records came out with his big band, they were sloppier than hell, and I just loved 'em! They were rip-roaring, whorehouse stuff, you know. Like, the very first record that he made with that big band was "Swingin' At The Daisy Chain." Well, I didn't know what a daisy chain was from... I'm from Spokane! And all of a sudden, here comes this thing. That's when I first heard Herschel, and then when Lester played that famous solo on "Time Out"... Oh, I think that's one of the greatest things I ever heard in my life.
And I'll always regret that I never got to meet Dick Wilson. I did get to know Don Byas pretty well. But I never got to know Pha Terrell. I did know Dan Grissom very
Rowles - 22

well. I got to know the guys in Lunceford's band very well, all of them. Joe Thomas is one of my best friends. And I worked with Willie Smith out in Los Angeles, when he just... before he was getting very sick.

The last time I saw him was when Charlie Barnet brought him into New York with a band he put together, a band here for Basin Street East, and Willie was the only guy he brought with him, you know, to play lead. That was the last time I saw him.

Well, see... The guys that worked with Harry James were working a very dangerous job, because it was the heaviest drinking band, outside of Casa Loma, in the world. And the heaviest drinker of the whole band was the leader. And between that and baseball, hard baseball, you didn't belong in the band. So consequently, Willie just turned into an out-and-out lush. I mean, good Lord, it was terrible. Of course, Lester Young would have drank 'em all out of the room.
And Harry was crazy about baseball.

Oh yeah. Everybody that had a car in that band, he opened up the case in the back -- there's the uniform and the cleats and the bats and the gloves... They weren't any good at it either. We played 'em one time and beat 'em.
Rowles - 23
What band was that?

Woody. Yeah, we beat 'em. Played the hard softball. That was funny. Boy, they were mad. They didn't think anybody could beat 'em; they were too good. I said, "You ain't too good. You're too busy at the bar."
[END OF TAPE 1, SIDE A]
When did you start getting interested in music? When did that happen?
Seriously, you mean?
Or at all.

See, we always had, in our house, like... Regardless of the old man, who was always in the kitchen with a straight shot and a bottle there, my mother used to listen to the... What the heck did they call that program? He'd sing things like "Mystery Of Life"... I'll think of it. And they'd sing all these beautiful, beautiful songs, like... I used to sit and listen to them. You know, I'd have my tennis racquet in my hand, and they were so pretty I'd just sit down on the davenport and listen to these things -- trees and... I learned all those tunes.

And my mother played the piano by ear, and I would always sit there and listen to her. But she knew all kinds
Rowles - 24
of songs, because she studied Classical guitar. And she was very good. Very good. She used to play piano by ear. And I used to listen to her, and I learned all the Classics from her.

Then I met this Indian, Blackfoot Indian out at Gonzaga University when I was studying pre-law. He was a musician, a real one. He was a genius. He came from a reservation, and nobody knows where he learned everything. But he played tenor saxophone, and he wrote arrangements without scores, and he had perfect pitch. He didn't a piano, it didn't mean anything to him. It was there in his head. And he heard me playing; I was trying to play like Freddie Kreitzer with Lombardo. I was in the gymnasium one day, playing. He came wandering in there -- I didn't know him...

He'd come over there on a scholarship. They had brought about six Indians over there -- some Sioux, Blackfoot, Nez Perce(?)... And they were my best friends! I liked them better than I liked anybody in the whole school.

And I remember Tony Canadeo(?) was there when I was there. Years and years later, I was in Los Angeles, and I was playing with my trio, and the team that he was playing was... What was it? The one that won for so many years. Canadeo and the big-time coach that was such a wheel... Bart Starr...you know who I'm talking about. Detroit? No, it
Rowles - 25
wasn't Detroit.
I have no idea. [VINCE LOMBARDI/GREEN BAY PACKERS]

Anyway, he was a backfield coach. So the owner of the club said... They were out... They had decided to celebrate at that club that night; they had won the Super Bowl. And they all came out there, see, and he was there. And I told the boss, you know; I said, "I went to school with that guy, Canadeo." I didn't know him, but I went to school with him. No-no. He went in the Army drunk. Marvelous, marvelous, marvelous... If I were to see him, if he were to walk in here this day, I'd kiss him and hug him. 'Cause I loved him. Everybody loved him. Everybody that knew him loved him. You had to understand him. These other guys that would come out there with blood in their eye, ready to blow him out because he didn't play like Hawkins, they didn't understand him. They didn't know what kind of a person... He was a different person.

You know, it's like when you're in high school and there's the guy with the glasses in the corner that always gets Straight-A in Science, and everybody puts him away, you know, and they won't talk to him and all that -- they don't
Rowles - 77

know how brilliant he is. I went to high school with a guy like that. I didn't talk to him... You couldn't talk to him. He was fifteen-twenty yards away from you before you had mentioned(?)... That's the way Lester was.

Lester had come in there to New York and he scared those guys just like Charlie Parker did! Ben Webster came back down... He heard about Charlie Parker and he went up to hear him, and he came back down to Birdland [sic] and he says, "Have you guys heard this Charlie Parker?" Now, he told me this himself. He says, "Well, you better get up there and listen to that. If you don't do that, you haven't lived. Wait'll you hear 'Cherokee.'" He says, "Holy God, there isn't anything on earth like that."

First thing you know, everybody in the town was playing Charlie Parker's style. And that's the reason why Charlie Parker went into dope heavy. Because every time he turned around and went into a club, he heard himself. Everybody was playing like Charlie Parker. They were all imitating. Sonny Stitt had him down, Jackie McLean was after his ass. Everybody was after the Bird. And the Bird was the Bird. And the Bird was a real nice guy!
I worked with him, and I took a trip with him, and I loaned him a white shirt with gun cufflinks. He brought them back to me. And he used to stand in the wings, and
Rowles - 78
he'd say, [RASPY] "Jimmy Rowles, 'There Will Never Be Another You' in B-flat. And he'd walk out and he'd start... I got along with him good.
I was very-very-very sad when I heard that he passed away. He passed away laughing, you know.
Watching TV, yeah.
Yeah, he was listening to Tommy Dorsey. He was up at the Countess. She must... You know, I like her.
I do, too.
I do, too. I think she's... All she's got left is Barry. And Barry is a beautiful guy, and he can play. Boy, he can play. Barry... I love Barry. He and I are good friends, thank God.

Thank God I'm good friends with all the piano players back here. I am better friends with the pianists in New York than I am with the pianists in Los Angeles. I don't know what it is about Los Angeles, but there is a jealousy of some kind or something like that. Like, you take guys like Lou Levy, who's the guy that's got the triple organ from...? Well, you just go through 'em. And it's bullshit. They don't give you credit, they won't accept credit.
Back here, I see Ronnie Matthews, he comes up and he says, "Hey, motherfucker." You know... Or this or that, you know. Or I see Ray Bryant or...
Rowles - 79
[PAUSE-PHONE]

But L.A. is a funny place. I don't know what it is. I like to live there. But the music, I don't like it. I like a lot of the conductors in Los Angeles. I think my favorite conductor in Los Angeles is Jack Elliott. I've played for under (you say you "play under," you know, when you play for a conductor) Earl Fagin, a very, very fine conductor. But I don't think he conducts any more. I think he had a couple of heart attacks. He is a very fine musician. Billy May. You have to learn everybody's downbeat, you know; it's all different. Hank Mancini's downbeat is a long downbeat. Billy May comes right down on it. There's different guys like that. Pete Rugolo, you never know what he's going to do. Johnny Mandel can't conduct for shit, and he knows it. He can write like a mother, but he can't conduct. And Nelson Riddle is a bad conductor. He's a great writer, but he's a... You've got to learn how to follow him. You've got to learn how to follow Franz Waxman. And Dmitri...
Tiomkin?
Yeah. Or whoever. All those guys. Alfred Newman, easy to follow. All those different guys. I never worked for those guys in New York. I didn't come to New York to do that stuff. I came to New York to
Rowles - 80
play Jazz. So I didn't run into any of those famous whatever they got back there. And I didn't even want to meet 'em. I'd just play what I damn well please.
Was there anything interesting about all of that studio work? You said yesterday that you got bored with it...
Oh!
But is there any kind of challenge in it?
Oh-ho-ho-ho...
No?

Challenge...!? You're up at six o'clock in the morning, you've got to drive all the way across town, clear across Coldwater Canyon, through Robinson's, out to Fox. And you park your car and you walk in, and you look at the piano. There's a great big stack of music. And here are the arrangers, and there's Lionel Newman... And thank God for Irving Thielman(?), he was there, because he could cover me when I couldn't cut it. Irving Thielman(?) gave me the greatest advice I ever had in my life about music. He said, 'Don't ever take yourself too seriously.' That's all he said. He could play anything at sight. [SIPS]

There were challenges, plenty of them. Boy. I used to go in there and walk in the studio, look at the music, said, 'Oh Jesus, I can't play this shit.' But somehow, I'd make it. How, I don't know. I'd go and study the saxophone
Rowles - 81
sections and see what they were up to, and see if they had anything to do with what I was doing. I would check the brass section, see where they were. And I'd have my piano parts with me.

Well, I became a studio musician. I went over. I taught myself how to read. I got so I could read pretty damn good! I'd look at something and I'd read it, and play. And Irving would say "Very good. Don't pay any attention to the fingering. Don't listen to your teacher, and hold your hands a certain way and all that crap. Just so it comes off. Just play it. Your own way. If it comes off, it comes off. If you can't play it, I'll cover you."

And Irving used to cover me. I saw Irving cover Yehudi Menuhin, the famous violinist. His accompanist couldn't cut it. And so Alfred was conducting, and Alfred says, "Take ten." And he says, "Irving, come here." And by now, Irving wasn't playing any more; he was the contractor, and he was on the phone all the time. So he got up and he came over and he says... He used to call Alfred Newman "Pappy."

Alfred Newman was a prince! He even used to take me into his private dressing room to give me a straight shot of something, pull me up. You know, he'd say, "Now, listen. You're the greatest cellist..." What did they call that thing that you play? Cello. Not cello... Celeste...
Rowles - 82
Oh yeah.

Celeste. He'd say, "You're the greatest celeste player in the world. Drink this. Now go out there and play that goddamn thing, and don't give me any shit." And I'd go out there and I'd play it! Then he'd stop me, TIP-TIP-TIP, everybody would shut up. He would say, "See, I told you."
Pappy. Bad cat. He was a (?). Except that he wasn't Czechoslovakian. He was a Jewish master. And I loved him dearly, in a fatherly way. Because I never had a father!

I had about six or seven fathers. I had Ben Webster, Benny Carter, Alfred Newman... There was a guy at Paramount, you know... Because my stepfather didn't understand music. But I don't want to be morbid. Let's change the subject. Quick. Let's go back to Rod Laver.
Let's talk a little bit about singers.
Singers.
Yeah.
All right. I can always talk about singers.
You have accompanied the greatest, and especially what people would think of as the three great ladies -- Billie, Ella and Sarah. What can an accompanist do for a singer, and how does he do it?
Well, the first thing you do is listen to her
Rowles - 83

sing. Hear how she sings. Then you try to play to make her happy. You don't play too much, you don't play enough, this, that, you know... And of course, all singers are crazy. Like George Shearing says, what's that famous thing he said...? "There are four sexes, male, female, homosexual and girl singers." And I think he said it right.
Incidentally, speaking of George Shearing, I think he is probably one of the finest solo pianists I have ever heard in my life. I admire George Shearing very much, and I like him personally.

But to get back to the singers... I played for so many singers, I can't even tell you... One of the finest, one of the best singers I ever played for wasn't a Jazz singer. That's the funny part of it. Evelyn Knight. She was a socialite type. She worked at the Palmer House, and this and that, you know... Boy, what a woman! She was something else. I loved that girl! And she sang songs like "Grandfather's Clock" and "A Little Bird Told Me That You..." -- and she didn't want me to do nothin' but just OMM-CHI, OOM-CHI, OOM-CHI. An occasional Count Basie; I could get away with that, that was all right. But if I started playing funny chords, whoa, she'd call me down. Otherwise, everything was completely together.
She had guys chasing her... She was a beautiful girl!
Rowles - 84

She had guys like Milt Raskin, or Milt...the guy that bought RKO, Milt Raxson(?) or whatever his name is... Kind of like that. Millionaires! Called her from all over the world, all the time: "Evelyn, please marry me. Marry me. Marry me." Then I'd knock on the door, and she'd say...hang up, and say, "Wait a minute. What do you want? Money? How much do you want?" She'd write me out a check. Then she'd say, "Now, watch. Don't play them funny chords behind me. They go after the show."
And then after the show, she'd sing Jazz! She'd sing "No More..." She's the only girl I ever played for that sang "No More," outside of Lady Day. Evelyn Knight. And I adored her. I loved her...!
Same for Carmen. She'd come out there and give you a bad time... Sings real great. But the personality part, forget it. She and I are friends, you know, but not close.

Sarah... I love Sarah. Nothin' wrong with Sarah. I think Sarah is the greatest singer... Without being a Classical singer, I would say that Sarah Vaughan is the greatest singer alive today. And if I was a younger man, I'd be after her for that job. But I couldn't keep up with her. I'm too old. I think Sarah Vaughan is probably, to me... I made one album with her. Have you heard that album?
Oh yes, I have it.
Rowles - 85
What do you think of that album?
Oh, I like it very much.

I think that's one of the best albums she ever made. You know, they left about three tracks off that album. She sang "...[SINGS]...and yet..." She sang that. And then we did... We played...just the two of us, we played. Well, I forget what that was. That wasn't on it. They didn't put that on it. Bobby Shad?
Yeah.
Yeah, I've heard... I almost jumped over his desk at him.
Well, he sold that label to...
Because we did "Morning Star," and it was my tune with Johnny Mercer's lyrics, and he put down...
W.C. Handy or something?
W.C. Handy. Boy, he's a bad cat. I'd like to meet him again some time. I've got sharp toes.
Yeah, Bobby... He's out of the record business, I think.

I understand he's escaped with a whole bunch of stuff. Stop. I wouldn't believe it. I wouldn't doubt it, I mean. Well, some day, maybe, if I'm lucky, I'll see him -- if I'll know him. If I do that, there will be a little violence in the place. Because I think that's one of
Rowles - 86
the best records Sarah ever made.
Yeah, it's a lovely record.
Oh, she went wild on "That Face." And the way she sang "The Folks On The Hill"... WSHEW.
She's amazing, because her voice hasn't lost anything. On the contrary...
It's gotten better and better and better. She's the greatest on earth, I think. And that includes the Classicals, like Leontyne Price and all that. I still think Sarah cuts everybody.
Oh yeah.
And did you ever hear her play the piano?
Yes.

She'll play that piano. She knows. You could play World War... I've said this before. You could have World War Three going on; she'd still sing. Sarah Vaughan... God gave us Sarah Vaughan. He's taken a lot of them younger away. But he's left Sarah Vaughan. I think He likes to sit up there and listen to her. Because I'm afraid he thinks that when he gets her up there, nobody can...she won't have any help. She's too good! I don't know what he did with Tatum. He could put Tatum on a separate cloud and let him go. But with Sarah, I don't know.

I have a Japanese name for Sarah. It means "miracle."
Rowles - 87

And the word is "kaiseki"(?). I've told a couple of people, like Susannah...you know Susannah Claude(?). I told her to walk up to Sarah and say "kaiseki"(?). And Sarah turned around and she said, "You've been talking to Jimmy."

But I adore her. I adore her. Personally. Everything. Every wise, every way. I think she is just... And her sense of humor is ridiculous, it's so much. She came to my house one night, and she saw these two little kittens playing, and she'd never seen this. Marshall was with her. And she said, "Marshall, I want two cats." She said, "What will I start with? I want two of the best." I said, "You might as well start at the top. Get a couple of Abyssinians." So next night, the phone rang. They paid seventy-five bucks a piece for two Abyssinians. And they had two Schnauzers. And they dropped these Abyssinians on the floor, and the Abyssinians immediately smothered the dogs. And the phone kept ringing' all night! It was hysterical! So she named one of them Haile and the other Selassie. Somebody stole one of them; either that or the coyotes got him. But the other one she's still got. I don't know whether it's Haile or Selassie.
But that's the reason why she got those cats, because she was at my house. And she played the piano that night, and boy, I wish I had a tape of that. Wow! She played some
Rowles - 88
stuff. She was just improvising. She's a beautiful, beautiful, beautiful woman.
Yes, I did a lot of things with her and played for her a lot. I played for Carmen quite a bit, but it wasn't like playing for Sarah. There's nothing like playing for Sarah or Lady Day.

When I used to work for Lady Day, it was like... I was a lot younger, you know, of course... It was like I couldn't wait to get there. I just couldn't wait to get there and see her and Pepe, her little dog. I'd go all the way up to his ears, and then he'd start snapping his teeth and I'd quit. Because he'd turn around and bite your hand if you went past his ears.
What kind of a dog was that? That wasn't the little boxer she had.
He was a Mexican Hairless or some damn thing. He was a little piece of shit that you could stick in a pinhole. But he was Pepe!

I was lucky, I think. I wasn't working with her when she was all strung out and all ...[VOLUME BRIEFLY DROPS DRAMATICALLY, TO INAUDIBILITY]... I was lucky. I worked for her when she was in California. I never travelled with her. But it's probably better. And the lawyer... Last night we met Earl, he was her lawyer for the last three years. And
Rowles - 89

he told me that she used to ask about me, talk about me. She said, 'I wish I had him, but I can't afford him.' And that just stopped me, that she would remember... 'I wish I had him, but I can't afford him.' But every time I'd come to California to record, BANG... And I was on all those records. Unless I was doing something else; they used Oscar.
You did all those nice things with Ben and Benny Carter and Sweets...

Yeah. Norman would never give me much of a chance. He had too many big stars there. I was just there. She wanted me there. That's all. As long as I was sitting at the piano, she was happy. She didn't give a shit whether I played a solo or what. I loved her.

segments.chapter: Spokane and arrival in Los Angeles
segments.title: Born in Spokane; stepfather and leaving for Los Angeles
segments.summary: Rowles was born in Spokane in 1918, his father died young and his stepfather wanted him to be a lawyer. At twenty-one he announced he was going to Los Angeles to play piano.

segments.chapter: Spokane and arrival in Los Angeles
segments.title: First months in Los Angeles and first steady job
segments.summary: He sat in at Hollywood and Watts clubs while living in a boarding house, then got his first steady trio job with a tenor and bass.

segments.chapter: Spokane and arrival in Los Angeles
segments.title: Slim and Slam trio, Herb Rose's club and Carlos Gastel buying Nat Cole's contract
segments.summary: Claire Fisher took him to hear Slim and Slam, who hired him. At Herb Rose's club he saw Carlos Gastel buy Nat Cole's contract for ten dollars.

segments.chapter: Spokane and arrival in Los Angeles
segments.title: Playing intermission piano for Tatum and becoming known
segments.summary: Herb Rose made him play intermission for Art Tatum, and he met Tatum and began to get a name around town.

segments.chapter: Billy Berg's band with Lee and Lester Young
segments.title: Billy Berg's big band at the Capri and the Trouville
segments.summary: Billy Berg hired him for a group with Slim and Slam, Lee and Lester Young and the Spirits of Rhythm, first at the Capri and then at the Trouville.

segments.chapter: Billy Berg's band with Lee and Lester Young
segments.title: Billie Holiday arrives and learning to accompany; Teddy Bear and Lester
segments.summary: Billie Holiday joined the band and taught him accompaniment; he describes her brother-sister friendship with Lester Young and recommends Lester's companion Teddy Bear.

segments.chapter: Billy Berg's band with Lee and Lester Young
segments.title: Lester Young blowing the visiting tenor players out
segments.summary: Illinois Jacquet, Don Byas, Ben Webster and others came with blood in their eye and Lester, half drunk, outplayed them all without a bad word.

segments.chapter: Goodman, Woody Herman and the Army
segments.title: Joining Benny Goodman through Ben Webster
segments.summary: Ben Webster and Jimmy Maxwell got him the Goodman job after Mel Powell left; Goodman's sciatica and ray made him hard to work with.

segments.chapter: Goodman, Woody Herman and the Army
segments.title: Woody Herman's band, the Army and returning to Woody
segments.summary: He quit Goodman for Woody Herman's cooperative band, was drafted for three years, and rejoined Woody on discharge until the band broke up.

segments.title: Freelance bands and turning down the Four Brothers band
segments.summary: He worked with Tommy Dorsey, Les Brown and Goodman, and refused to rejoin Woody because of the road and the drug use, as Herb Steward also left.

segments.title: Bob Crosby radio show, recording and entering the studios
segments.summary: Jerry Gray's call for the Bob Crosby show led to recording, and a trip with Peggy Lee led to Alfred Newman and Fox, making him a busy studio man.

segments.title: Seventeen years as Henry Mancini's pianist and other studio work
segments.summary: He was Mancini's pianist for seventeen years on pictures, albums and concerts, alongside jingles and dates for Riddle, May and Rugolo, and a staff job at NBC.

segments.title: Forming his own trio: Mitchell, Bennett, Simpkins, Budwig, Bailey
segments.summary: His Sunday and Monday trio went through many bass players and drummers, including Frank Butler, until Monty Budwig and Donald Bailey made his best trio.

segments.title: Working with singers: Peggy Lee, Andy Williams, Vic Damone
segments.summary: He accompanied Peggy Lee for about five years, then Andy Williams and many other singers around Los Angeles.

segments.title: Sarah Vaughan and Carmen McRae sing with his trio; records with them
segments.summary: At his Manhattan Beach job, Sarah Vaughan and Carmen McRae sat in, and he made albums with each.

segments.title: Amsterdam concert, visiting Ben Webster in Copenhagen and his death
segments.summary: On a tour with Sarah he took time off to visit Ben Webster in Copenhagen, and soon after Ben died; Rowles says Ben was like a father.

segments.title: Leaving the studios for New York: Tatum tribute, the Cookery and Bradley's
segments.summary: He played the Art Tatum tribute at the Jazz Festival, then the Cookery and Bradley's and spent years in New York.

segments.title: Touring with Ella Fitzgerald and emphysema
segments.summary: Norman Granz hired him for Ella; the travel nearly killed him, he developed emphysema and quit.

segments.title: Playing with his daughter Stacy and how she took up trumpet
segments.summary: His daughter Stacy inspired him to play again; he tells how she found his old trumpet, learned it and became a flugelhorn soloist.

segments.title: Early love of Guy Lombardo and Hal Kemp, then Count Basie's records
segments.summary: As a boy he idolised Lombardo and Freddie Kreitzer, liked Hal Kemp's crispness, and was thrilled by Basie's first sloppy big band records and Lester's solo.

segments.title: Lunceford's band, Willie Smith and Harry James's baseball
segments.summary: He knew many Lunceford players and singers, and recalls Willie Smith's drinking in the Harry James band and Woody's band beating them at softball.

segments.title: Music in the house: his mother's piano and guitar
segments.summary: Radio music and his mother's by-ear piano and classical guitar were how he learned early tunes.

segments.title: Blackfoot musician and Native students at Gonzaga
segments.summary: At Gonzaga he befriended a brilliant Blackfoot tenor saxophonist and other Native students.

segments.title: Tony Canadeo and the Packers at the club
segments.summary: A story of meeting football player Tony Canadeo, a Gonzaga classmate, at a Los Angeles club, and Rowles's contempt for him.

segments.title: The Blackfoot friend plays him Teddy Wilson and changes his life
segments.summary: His friend played him Benny Goodman's trio record with Teddy Wilson, after which Rowles collected Wilson, Basie, Fats Waller, Ellington and Lunceford records.

segments.title: Self-taught, and Joe Thomas getting him started at Casa Manana
segments.summary: He never played in a school band and taught himself to read; Joe Thomas of Lunceford's band, whom he met in Seattle, helped him on arrival in California.

segments.title: Seattle's Jackson Street scene
segments.summary: He spent time in Seattle playing all night on Jackson Street, learning from Julian Hanson, and was accepted by visiting musicians.

segments.chapter: Ben Webster, Tatum and Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Ellington in Seattle: Ben Webster, Blanton, Strayhorn and stride piano
segments.summary: When Ellington played Seattle, he became close to Ben Webster, played with Blanton, and Ben introduced him to stride pianists.

segments.chapter: Ben Webster, Tatum and Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Art Tatum's encouragement and Slam Stewart
segments.summary: Tatum took him around and told him to be himself; he describes Tatum's handicap, forming of the trio with Slam Stewart and Tiny Grimes.

segments.chapter: Ben Webster, Tatum and Los Angeles scene
segments.title: George Mraz and the nickname Bounce
segments.summary: He explains his nickname for bassist George Mraz.

segments.chapter: Ben Webster, Tatum and Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Lester's nicknames and being the only white man in the band
segments.summary: Lester called him Gray Boy; he was the only white player and was teased about a conk.

segments.chapter: Ben Webster, Tatum and Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Race: no problems then; opinion on violence
segments.summary: He says there were no race problems in the early 1940s, voices views on Martin Luther King and violence, and says he preferred Black musicians.

segments.chapter: Ben Webster, Tatum and Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Central Avenue and Watts clubs, mixed audiences
segments.summary: He describes the mixed audiences and after-hours clubs of Central Avenue, where he met Earl Hines and Barney Kessel.

segments.chapter: Ben Webster, Tatum and Los Angeles scene
segments.title: Jimmy Blanton's bass playing and death
segments.summary: He describes Blanton's revolutionary bass, his friendship with Ben Webster, and visiting Blanton in the sanitarium with TB.

segments.chapter: Lee and Lester Young band remembered
segments.title: Lee Young as leader; writing for the band; why Lester left Basie
segments.summary: Lee Young led the band and was the sole abstainer; Rowles wrote charts, Lester kept his part in his pocket, and nobody knows why he left Basie.

segments.chapter: Lee and Lester Young band remembered
segments.title: Pause and sake
segments.summary: The interview pauses for drinks.

segments.chapter: Lee and Lester Young band remembered
segments.title: Leo Watson of the Spirits of Rhythm
segments.summary: Rowles describes Leo Watson's looks, drumming and wisecracks at the Capri.

segments.chapter: Lee and Lester Young band remembered
segments.title: Stokowski and the movie stars at the Capri
segments.summary: Leopold Stokowski and many Hollywood actors came to the Capri to watch Leo and the dancers.

segments.chapter: Lee and Lester Young band remembered
segments.title: Dancer Marie Bryant
segments.summary: He praises the dancing of Marie Bryant.

segments.chapter: Lee and Lester Young band remembered
segments.title: Billie Holiday in Los Angeles: Bumps, Jimmy Monroe and recording with her
segments.summary: Billie fell for Bumps Myers and a man named Monroe rather than Lester; Rowles recalls her friendship with Lester and recording with her many times.

segments.title: Jimmie Lunceford's death
segments.summary: He and the interviewer discuss how Lunceford died, and Stanley Dance.

segments.title: Lunceford's band at Casa Manana and Eddie Wilcox's arrangements
segments.summary: Rowles thinks the Lunceford band outplayed everyone and credits Eddie Wilcox with many arrangements.

segments.title: Sake is served
segments.summary: Drinks arrive and Stacy shoos them away.

segments.title: Lunceford's twelve-chorus arrangement and Mr. Kennedy's destroyed records
segments.summary: He recalls a Lunceford arrangement with twelve out-choruses and a collector who blew up his disc recordings.

segments.title: BMI-era songs, Ellington's 1960s records, Mercer Ellington
segments.summary: They talk about BMI tunes and Ellington's recordings and Duke's treatment of Mercer.

segments.title: Sweet singers Dan Grissom and Pha Terrell
segments.summary: He defends sweet band singers and recalls accompanying Grissom in Seattle.

segments.title: Billy May's Lunceford tribute record
segments.summary: Billy May transcribed the Lunceford arrangements and Joe Thomas praised him.

segments.title: Don Brown, the Blackfoot arranger, and his later life
segments.summary: He tells how Don Brown copied Lunceford's Frisco Fog by ear and of his decline.

segments.title: Break: dinner plans and the evening's gig
segments.summary: Rowles talks with Stacy about dinner and the evening's work.

segments.title: Athletics and a bad-tempered Jerry Gray on the road
segments.summary: He boasts of his athleticism and recalls Jerry Gray forcing the radio band on the road.

segments.title: Ice skating as a boy and on the road
segments.summary: He tells of boyhood skating and of skating with the band behind a gymnasium.

segments.title: Tennis: women players of the day
segments.summary: He opines on McEnroe and women tennis players and the greats he watched.

segments.title: Tennis and jazz: serves and age
segments.summary: He compares tennis rhythm to jazz and talks about Rosewall, Tanner and watching matches.

segments.title: Pancho Gonzalez, McEnroe and Nastase tempers
segments.summary: A story of Pancho Gonzalez taking a woman's hat with a ball.

segments.title: Placido Domingo at Bradley's
segments.summary: He tells how he met Placido Domingo at Bradley's and joked about doing an opera together.

segments.title: Peggy Lee gets him singing
segments.summary: Peggy Lee heard him sing on a Vegas trip and encouraged him.

segments.title: Army NCO club band; Dick Libertini; Bob Preston
segments.summary: He played at an Army NCO club and mentions Dick Libertini and Bob Preston.

segments.title: Recording a calypso album with Robert Mitchum
segments.summary: He describes weeks of rehearsal with Mitchum and Gene DePaul.

segments.title: Smoking, drinking and smoky clubs
segments.summary: He talks about cigarettes and smoke in clubs like Bradley's.

segments.title: Sake instead of vodka; playing in Japan
segments.summary: He prefers sake and praises Japanese audiences.

segments.title: Applause covering solos; Prez asking for titty-boom
segments.summary: They talk about applause, and Lester told a drummer to play very lightly.

segments.title: Cooking contest and Lester Young's room
segments.summary: He recalls a cooking contest and visiting Lester's room with his record stack.

segments.title: Lester Young as a unique person; his father and family
segments.summary: He calls Lester the most unique person he knew and tells of Lester's father and a move to Teddy's house.

segments.title: Lester's drinking and why he was misunderstood
segments.summary: Lester was always a heavy drinker, and rivals misunderstood him.

segments.title: Charlie Parker
segments.summary: Ben Webster told him about Parker, imitation drove Bird into drugs, and Rowles worked with him.

segments.summary: He is closer to New York pianists than Los Angeles ones.

segments.title: Los Angeles conductors and their downbeats
segments.summary: He rates conductors such as Billy May, Mancini, Rugolo and Newman.

segments.title: Studio work at Fox: Irving Thielman and Alfred Newman
segments.summary: He describes the challenge of studio sight-reading, Irving Thielman's advice, and Alfred Newman as father figure.

segments.title: What an accompanist does for a singer
segments.summary: Asked about Billie, Ella and Sarah, he says to listen to the singer, and praises Shearing.

segments.title: Evelyn Knight and Carmen McRae
